periods.analysis: Harborview opens this series in a strong green position: Population Growth Rate is 2.2%, comfortably above the >= 1.5% target and a clear signal that our coastal gateway economy is still pulling households toward opportunity. Planning’s quarterly Address Point Reconciliation, using utility starts from HVW-UTL route books 12, 18, and 27 plus airport-area certificate-of-occupancy records, shows growth concentrated in the East Basin, North Harbor, and Bayside Station corridors. That is good news for Council’s economic vitality story, and it also confirms why our reporting calendar matters: fast growth only helps residents if we keep housing, water-main renewal, school attendance partners, and flood-resilience work synchronized.
periods.recommendations: Sustain the green by locking the Q4 population file by the 5th business day after quarter close, with Planning, Utilities, and Permitting signing off on the same address universe. Extend the East Basin and Bayside Station dashboard cuts so Council can see where growth is converting into occupied units, not just permitted units. Keep a watch-item on affordability pressure by pairing this measure with multifamily completions and eviction-prevention intake in the next council packet.

periods.analysis: Population Growth Rate finished Q4 at 1.9%, down 0.3 percentage points from 2.2% in 2024-Q3, but still green and above the >= 1.5% target. The movement is seasonally sensible: Harborview usually sees fewer household moves in November and December, and the permit team noted that two North Harbor mixed-use buildings shifted final inspections into January rather than closing in December. The underlying signal remains healthy, with seaport logistics hiring and airport concession expansions continuing to support in-migration. I would describe this to Council as moderated growth, not softness, with the usual friendly nudge that our data-quality checks need to stay tight during holiday reporting cycles.
periods.recommendations: Sustain performance by completing the delayed North Harbor occupancy validation before the Q1 scorecard freeze, including parcel IDs NH-44A and NH-52C. Ask Permitting to flag any certificate-of-occupancy slippage over 30 days so we can distinguish construction timing from actual population demand. Extend the quarterly narrative cross-check with the Housing Office, because green growth is only a win if residents can find attainable units near jobs and transit.

periods.analysis: Population Growth Rate rebounded to 2.1% in 2025-Q1, up 0.2 percentage points from 1.9% in 2024-Q4 and still green against the >= 1.5% target. The January carryover from North Harbor came through, and Planning’s match to new water accounts on mains W-31 and W-32 helped cleanly confirm occupied units rather than just paper completions. The rebound fits the broader Harborview pattern: airport cargo hiring, medical district expansion, and small-business openings along Route 6 are translating into steady household formation. The one data note I would keep visible is that growth is arriving fastest in corridors where water-main age and tidal-street flooding already compete for capital attention.
periods.recommendations: Sustain the green by publishing the Q1 validated address file to departments no later than April 12, so Finance, Utilities, and the Housing Office are working from the same base. Extend the Route 6 corridor cut to include school attendance-zone overlays, giving our chronic-absenteeism partners an early view of student movement. Keep the Pipeline Renewal coordination active for W-31 and W-32 service-area growth so new demand does not get ahead of older pipe constraints.

periods.analysis: Harborview accelerated again in 2025-Q2, with Population Growth Rate at 2.3%, up 0.2 percentage points from 2.1% in 2025-Q1 and well above the >= 1.5% target. This is our strongest point in the current arc so far, helped by the May lease-up of Harborline Apartments, the Portside Workforce Homes phase, and new employee cohorts tied to Terminal 4 and the international airport concourse program. The green result is exactly the kind of momentum we want to show Council: a thriving city, an AA-rated balance sheet, and neighborhoods that remain attractive to workers, families, and entrepreneurs. The operational caveat is capacity discipline, especially around permit closeout queues, shelter outreach demand near the transit center, and flood-prone blocks in South Tidal Village.
periods.recommendations: Sustain the green by adding a mid-quarter permit-to-occupancy pulse check for large buildings over 75 units, starting with Harborline, Portside, and Bayside Lofts. Extend the population-growth map to show transit walksheds and stormwater hot spots, so growth decisions are tied to service readiness. For the Council work session, pair this measure with housing production and homelessness outreach placements to keep the prosperity story honest and actionable.

periods.analysis: Population Growth Rate held very strong at 2.2% in 2025-Q3, down 0.1 percentage points from 2.3% in 2025-Q2 and still green against the >= 1.5% target. That small easing looks like normalization after the Q2 lease-up surge, not a loss of momentum, because utility starts, school enrollment adds, and USPS delivery-point changes all moved in the same direction. The strongest adds remain in East Basin, Bayside Station, and the airport employment shed, with a quieter but important uptick in accessory dwelling unit completions in Old Marina. From a scorecard perspective, this is a clean, defensible result: high growth, good corroborating data, and no need to overstate the story.
periods.recommendations: Sustain performance by keeping the three-source validation standard in place: utility starts, certificate-of-occupancy records, and delivery-point changes must reconcile before the dashboard is marked final. Extend the Old Marina ADU review with a small owner survey through the Neighborhood Services team, because those units are helping absorb growth without major infrastructure disruption. Continue briefing Utilities on East Basin demand so Pipeline Renewal sequencing stays aligned with where population is actually landing.

periods.analysis: Population Growth Rate moved to 1.9% in 2025-Q4, down 0.3 percentage points from 2.2% in 2025-Q3, while remaining green and above the >= 1.5% target. This mirrors the prior year’s Q4 seasonal moderation, and the data team confirmed the same basic driver: fewer household moves late in the year plus several final inspections held for January closeout. The city’s fundamentals remain strong, with port logistics, health care, and neighborhood retail still supporting demand, but Q4 is the right moment to be disciplined rather than celebratory. For Council, I would frame this as sustained green growth with a predictable winter dip and a clear watch on affordability and service capacity.
periods.recommendations: Sustain the green by pre-scheduling the January occupancy reconciliation now, not after the holidays, with named owners from Planning, Permitting, Utilities, and IT. Extend the Q4 review to include stalled permits over 45 days so we can remove administrative friction where projects are ready to house people. Keep the affordability watch-item in the public packet by showing median rent movement beside the 1.9% growth result.

periods.analysis: Population Growth Rate returned to 2.1% in 2026-Q1, up 0.2 percentage points from 1.9% in 2025-Q4 and green against the >= 1.5% target. The rebound is consistent with the now-established Harborview pattern: winter moderation followed by first-quarter move-ins as delayed inspections, employer relocations, and spring leasing activity clear. Planning’s data-quality note is positive this quarter, because the Civic Analytics team resolved duplicate address records in the Harbor Gateway subdivision file before the scorecard deadline. The growth story remains strong, but I am keeping the friendly nudge on cross-department readiness because the same neighborhoods gaining residents are also asking about water reliability, school attendance supports, and flood-day access routes.
periods.recommendations: Sustain the green by making the duplicate-address check a standard step in the Q2 close process, with the Harbor Gateway script saved in the ClearPoint evidence library. Extend coordination with the School District attendance team by sending them the updated growth-by-census-block file before their summer intervention roster is finalized. Ask Public Works to compare Q1 growth hot spots with Pipeline Renewal segments PR-17 and PR-22 so capital timing stays credible.

periods.analysis: Harborview closed 2026-Q2 at 2.3% Population Growth Rate, up 0.2 percentage points from 2.1% in 2026-Q1 and well above the >= 1.5% target. This matches the prior year’s Q2 high point and gives us a strong two-year arc: recurring seasonal dips, reliable rebounds, and growth consistently above target. The operational detail behind the number is encouraging, with South Harbor Commons, Concourse Village phase 2, and 38 ADU finals contributing to occupied-unit gains verified through utility account activation. The status is green and confidence is warranted, but the responsible message to Council is that thriving growth now requires equally steady execution on housing affordability, homelessness pathways, tidal resilience, and aging water assets.
periods.recommendations: Sustain the green by continuing the Q2 large-project occupancy huddle and adding South Harbor Commons and Concourse Village phase 2 to the standing agenda. Extend the measure for the next cycle with a simple growth-capacity appendix: occupied units, water-main risk segments, flood-access routes, and affordable-unit completions. For the next Council update, lead with the 2.3% result, then show the concrete service-readiness actions so the public sees growth being managed, not merely counted.

periods.analysis: Population growth is above target at 1.31%, but rent burden is rising and Downtown Waterfront Revitalization remains below plan. Growth is favorable; readiness and affordability are not settled.
periods.recommendations: Pair the growth result with housing, utility-capacity and waterfront delivery risks in the Council summary.
